newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Northern Afghan chief urges Taleban to share power.
newsitem.headline: Northern Afghan chief urges Taleban to share power.

text.p: Northern opposition leader General Abdul Malik said on Sunday the Islamic Taleban militia must share power to bring peace to Afghanistan.

"When a central government has been established with the participation of all nationalities and tribes in Afghanistan, then we will obey that government," Malik told reporters in his ethnic Uzbek-dominated stronghold of Mazar-i-Sharif.
"We do not want the north as an independent country. We want a united Afghanistan, but we want due representation for all nationalities residing in the country," he added.

Three weeks ago, the 35-year-old Malik, then a key commander in the opposition forces of former communist General Abdul Rashid Dostum, defected to the mainly ethnic Pashtun Taleban and with their help drove Dostum from Mazar-i-Sharif.
Three days later, he turned on his new allies and, after fierce battles that left at least 300 dead, forced them to flee.
Malik said he had attacked the Taleban because they had broken promises not to interfere in the internal administration of the north or to disarm his ethnic Uzbek troops.
"We had come to an arrangement with the Taleban for the establishment of peace and a broad-based government, to impose Islamic law and to ensure the country's territorial integrity.

"But the Taleban agreed not to interfere in the affairs of the northern government or to disarm their forces. They broke the agreement," said the soft-spoken general, wearing a purple jacket, floral tie and trousers -- a change from the green robes he wore while his alliance with the Taleban was intact.
Malik said he was willing to negotiate with the Taleban and had asked Afghanistan's neighbours to mediate.
"We have called on all neighbouring countries to mediate between us and the Taleban," he said, adding that a negotiated peace was the only solution to Afghanistan's problems.
Malik said there had been no contact with the Islamic militia since Mazar-i-Sharif changed hands.
His statement appeared to contradict that of a Pakistani Foreign Ministry official who said on Friday that Islamabad had been passing messages between Malik and the Taleban.
"There has been no contact," Malik declared. "So far they (the Taleban) have been regrouping and recruiting to continue the war. They want a military solution to the conflict."
He threatened to kill Taleban prisoners, believed to include the militia's foreign minister, northern military chief and central bank governor, if the north was attacked.

"Approximately 10,000 Taleban prisoners have been taken in the north. If the Taleban persist in fighting, the lives of the prisoners will be in danger and the responsibility will rest with them," he said.
However, Malik said the Taleban should not let their losses in the north stand in the way of rapprochement.
"The Taleban imposed the war and in war it's kill or be killed. If we count the dead on both sides, there will never be a solution to Afghanistan's problems. We must forgive."

But there are still major policy differences between the two sides. In the areas of Afghanistan they control, the Taleban have banned girls and women from schools and the workplace, a policy that Malik said was unacceptable in the north.
"We don't want the kind of society the Taleban want. We have Islamic scholars in the north who have approved women's rights to education and work. We will defend those rights," he said.
